prompt: Write a science fiction short story about first contact. About 800 words. Output only the story, with no title.
raw:
The signal came on a Tuesday, which Dr. Amara Okafor always thought was a strange day for history to happen.

She was alone at the listening station in the Mojave, the night shift nobody wanted, watching waveforms scroll across her monitor like the EKG of a sleeping world. Three years she'd worked this post, cataloging pulsars and satellite chatter and the occasional eccentric blip that always turned out to be a student's malfunctioning cube sat.

At 3:17 a.m., the waveform changed.

It wasn't noise. Noise is random, fecund, shapeless. This was pattern—prime numbers, she realized, when she pulled up the analysis: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, broadcast on the hydrogen line with a patience that suggested it had been repeating for a very long time. Her hands shook so badly she mistyped her supervisor's number twice.

Within six hours, the station was swarming. Within six days, so was the world. But that first night, for three hours and forty minutes before anyone official arrived, Amara had the signal to herself. She decoded what she could, and what she found was not what anyone expected.

Beneath the primes, layered like a message in a bottle within a message in a bottle, was arithmetic. Then geometry. Then, painstakingly, a primer—thousands of images accompanied by data strings, the kind of curriculum scientists had theorized an alien species might send. Diagrams of a star. Orbits. A planet with two shallow green seas. And then, near the end, something that stopped her breath: a sequence showing their sun swelling, red and monstrous, swallowing the inner orbits one by one.

The final image was a single symbol, repeated. She spent the rest of her life learning what it meant, but that night, staring at it in the desert dark, she understood intuitively: *Remember us.*

They weren't calling. There was no request in the signal, no question, no greeting awaiting reply. The message was almost seventy years old—it had left its dying world when Amara's grandmother was a girl. Whoever sent it, whatever they were, had known they wouldn't survive long enough for a conversation. The round trip to Earth and back would take a century and a half, and their planet had perhaps decades.

They weren't calling. They were whispering into the dark, the way you touch a photograph before a house fire, the way you carve your name into a bench you'll never sit on again.

The world's governments convened, of course. Committ`es formed, telescopes were commandeered, linguists and physicists and poets were recruited. Humanity composed a reply with the gravity of people writing a eulogy backward in time—a message that would arrive at a grave. We sent them music. We sent the structure of DNA, photographs of oceans, children's drawings collected from every continent. We sent our own primes, our own orbits, our own address in the galaxy. And we sent their symbol back to them, plus one: *You are remembered.*

Amara was seventy-three when the reply finished its long journey home to nowhere. She watched the transmission data confirm itself on a screen much thinner than her old monitor, and she wept, though she couldn't have said whether from grief or something closer to gratitude.

"It's strange," her granddaughter said, visiting her that evening. "We talk about it like it was a conversation. But they never heard us. They died before we even knew they existed."

"What is a conversation," Amara asked, "if not one voice, then another, across a silence?"

The girl thought about this. "Across eighty light-years of silence."

"All silences are distance," Amara said. "The ones between stars just happen to be measurable."

She lived long enough to see the monuments built—not to the aliens, who remained images of light and guesswork, but to the exchange itself. In Lagos, in Lima, in Novosibirsk, the symbol appeared on walls and school buildings and the sides of hospitals: their word for *remember us*, adopted by a species that had needed a stranger's dying whisper to teach it how to grieve for strangers.

The signal still repeats, every eleven hours, patient as it has always been. Children learn about it in school. Most of them can recite the sequence of the primer by heart—star, orbits, seas, dying sun, symbol. There are those who argue we should stop listening, that seventy years of a ghost's voice is enough, that humanity has its own future to attend to. They are, perhaps, not wrong.

But every year on the anniversary, the listening stations go quiet, all of them at once, so that nothing humanity makes will drown out those eleven hours. And people pause—busy people, tired people, people in traffic and kitchens and hospitals—and they listen, or simply remember listening.

Somewhere, in the space between stars, a whisper travels on at the speed of light, growing fainter by the parsec, carrying a civilization's last word.

And somewhere behind it, following the same path, our answer.
